clue.text: Rang in and registered

parts.note: a clock that rang the hour struck it
to be in is to be at home

explanation.surface: Someone phoned in and signed up for something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rang in' reads as one phrasal verb about phoning, but it splits: a clock rings, or strikes, and being in means being at home.
explanation.definitionFit: A remark that hits its target and makes a lasting impression on the listener has registered with them.

clue.text: Axe to cause devastation

definitions.meaning: first meaning: dismiss someone from their job
second meaning: plunder and lay waste a captured town

explanation.surface: Someone takes an axe to a place to wreck it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Axe' looks like the tool doing the damage, but it is the verb meaning to fire an employee.
explanation.definitionFit: Firing a worker and looting a conquered city are both expressed by the same short verb in English.

clue.text: Spellbound, hearing hit

indicators.note: on hearing a word we catch only its sound, not its spelling

parts.note: to hit is to rap, so 'hit' in the past tense is rapped

explanation.surface: Someone is entranced on hearing a hit song.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hit' suggests a chart song that holds the listener, but it is the past tense of the verb meaning to strike.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone completely absorbed and fascinated, unable to look away, is in a state of total engrossment.

clue.text: I'm unwilling to delegate? Surprisingly not, for a clerk

indicators.note: a surprising outcome is an unexpected arrangement, so the letters turn up in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A manager admits they won't hand work to a clerk, which is no surprise.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half is a remark the answer might make about itself, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who insists on managing every detail personally refuses to hand tasks to others, so this line is their typical attitude.

clue.text: Travel towards cape with French soldiers

indicators.note: with means together alongside, so the parts sit next to each other in turn

parts.note: a headland, as in Beachy Head, is a cape
F is the abbreviation for French
OR stands for other ranks, ordinary soldiers

explanation.surface: An expedition sets out for a cape alongside French troops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'French soldiers' looks like one unit, perhaps the Foreign Legion, but splits into an abbreviation and the usual crossword term for rank-and-file troops.
explanation.definitionFit: To set a course and move in the direction of a place is the phrasal verb meaning go there.

clue.text: Primarily: movie actress expressing witty enticements (singer, too!)

definitions.text: movie actress expressing witty enticements (singer, too!)

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so each word gives up its opening letter

parts.note: opening letter
opening letter
opening letter
opening letter
opening letter
opening letter
opening letter

explanation.surface: A thumbnail sketch of a film star famed for saucy one-liners who also sang.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue both describes the star and spells her name with its initials.
explanation.definitionFit: The American screen star of the 1930s was famous for suggestive wisecracks and also recorded songs and performed in vaudeville.

clue.text: Naked workers' protest in capital city

indicators.note: something naked has had its covering stripped, so the outer edges come away

parts.note: a go-slow is industrial action where staff deliberately work slowly

explanation.surface: Workers stage a nude demonstration in a capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Naked' suggests a nude protest, but it means stripping the first and last letters.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the seat of government and largest city of Norway, so it is a national capital.

clue.text: Kate's slightly corrupt, pursuing amphetamine: it makes you go faster

indicators.note: to pursue is to come behind, so this part follows the other

parts.note: speed is slang for amphetamine

indicators.note: corrupt means spoilt or tampered with, so the letters are disturbed from their order

parts.note: taken as written, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: Kate, a little crooked, is taking amphetamines to give her a buzz.
explanation.walkthrough: The drug talk primes a stimulant reading of the last part, but the definition is a piece of sports kit.
explanation.definitionFit: A long-bladed ice boot built for racing lets the wearer travel more quickly than ordinary skates.

clue.text: Where to find an old song with little effort

definitions.text: Where to find an old song
definitions.meaning: first meaning: platter is old slang for a gramophone record, where songs were once stored
second meaning: handed over without having to work for it

explanation.surface: Someone tracks down an old tune without much trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Platter' was mid-century slang for a vinyl disc, so a song is literally found on one.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom, often 'handed to you on a plate', describes getting something easily without having to strive.

clue.text: Change… open up, seeing European city

indicators.note: up suggests something stirred or churned up, so the letters are mixed

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A traveller resolves to change and open up after a trip to a European city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Change' looks like the anagram signal, but it is fodder; 'up' does that job.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the capital of Denmark and so one of the major urban centres of the continent.

clue.text: Tibetan's hiding letter from Greece

indicators.note: to hide something is to keep it concealed inside, so the word sits within the text

parts.note: the letters run inside this word

explanation.surface: A Tibetan conceals a letter sent from Greece.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests secret correspondence; 'letter' is an alphabet character.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the second character of the alphabet used in Greek writing, after alpha.

clue.text: Teenager Nick translated classical language

indicators.note: translating turns words into another form, so the letters are converted into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A schoolboy called Nick has translated a passage from a classical language.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Translated' fits the homework picture perfectly, which hides its job as the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The tongue of Homer and Plato is studied alongside Latin as one of the two classical languages of Western schooling.

clue.text: A real fan, ardent youth returned to see sports champ

indicators.note: ardent means fiery and passionate, so the letters are heated into a new shape

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: returned means sent back the way it came, so the word runs backwards

parts.note: a lad is a youth

explanation.surface: A keen young supporter came back to watch a sporting hero.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fan, ardent' reads as a description of the youth; 'ardent' is in fact the signal to rework the first three words.
explanation.definitionFit: The Spanish tennis star won twenty-two Grand Slam singles titles, a record fourteen of them at the French Open.

clue.text: Everyman's attitude leading to ultimately tedious tricks

indicators.note: to lead to something is to go in front, so the parts follow on in sequence

parts.note: the setter speaking of himself says I am, shortened to I'm
a posture is a stance or attitude

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is used

parts.note: final letter

explanation.surface: The setter's manner results in boring crossword trickery.
explanation.walkthrough: A setter naming himself in a clue usually stands for I or ME; here 'Everyman's' is Everyman is, giving I'M.
explanation.definitionFit: Deceptions in which someone pretends to be what they are not are frauds, so these are deceitful ruses.

clue.text: Real idiots misrepresented newspaper's stances

indicators.note: misrepresenting gives a distorted account, so the letters are presented out of order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Genuine fools have twisted what a paper stands for.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a complaint about a newspaper being misquoted; 'misrepresented' is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Leading articles are where a paper sets out its official opinion on the issues of the day.

clue.text: Busybody announced: 'Fruit'

indicators.note: something announced is spoken out, so we go by the sound

parts.note: a medlar is a small brown fruit eaten when half rotten

explanation.surface: A nosy neighbour makes a pronouncement about fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fruit' looks like what the busybody is talking about; it is the word to say aloud. The medlar is an old-fashioned fruit rarely seen in shops.
explanation.definitionFit: A busybody pokes into other people's affairs uninvited, which is exactly what interfering means.

clue.text: Knitter knitted a little ornament

indicators.note: knitting loops strands into a new pattern, so the letters are worked into another order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone who knits has made a small decoration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knitted' feels like the craft verb that goes with 'Knitter'; it is the signal to rearrange that word.
explanation.definitionFit: A cheap small decorative object or piece of jewellery of little value is called a bauble or knick-knack.

clue.text: Some confront a rioter somewhere in Canada

indicators.note: some means only a part, so the word is a portion of the text

parts.note: the letters run across these words

explanation.surface: Police face down a troublemaker at an unnamed spot in Canada.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' reads as an unspecified number of confrontations, but it signals a part of the text carrying the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a large Canadian province containing Toronto and Ottawa, so it is one location in the country.

clue.text: Outdoor revival of Pinafore fellow's skipped

indicators.note: a revival is a new staging, so the letters are put on in a fresh order
something skipped is passed over and left out

parts.note: HMS Pinafore is a Gilbert and Sullivan comic opera
F is the abbreviation for fellow

explanation.surface: A new outdoor production of the operetta has missed out one character's part.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revival' fits the theatre picture so well that it hides its job as the anagram signal, applied once the F is removed.
explanation.definitionFit: Something held outside rather than inside a building, like a summer concert in a park, is held al fresco.

clue.text: Chap, amateur one holding ball for marine creature

parts.note: a chap is a man
A is the abbreviation for amateur
a golf tee is the peg that holds the ball up

explanation.surface: A man, a novice cricketer perhaps, is holding the ball.
explanation.walkthrough: 'holding' tempts you to put one piece inside another, but 'one holding ball' is a single description of a golfer's peg.
explanation.definitionFit: The sea cow is a large slow plant-eating mammal living in warm coastal waters and rivers.

clue.text: Women bowlers aspire to these

definitions.meaning: second meaning: in cricket, an over in which the bowler concedes no runs

explanation.surface: Female bowlers have something they hope to achieve.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Women bowlers' reads as one phrase about a ladies' team; the split comes after 'Women'. In cricket a maiden over is six balls bowled without a run scored.
explanation.definitionFit: The old word for girls also names the cricket over yielding zero runs, a bowler's goal.

clue.text: Carrying a big stick, up there, out of the blue?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: menacing others with force, as in 'speak softly and carry a big stick'

definitions.text: up there, out of the blue?
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the sky overhead, no longer blue, promising a storm

explanation.surface: Someone wielding a club appears suddenly from above.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of the blue' means suddenly, but here it is literal: the sky has lost its blue and turned stormy.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes both intimidating behaviour and dark skies that look as if rain is imminent.

clue.text: Written up plans for undesired messages

indicators.note: in a down entry, writing upwards means the word reads bottom to top

parts.note: maps are plans of an area

explanation.surface: Proposals drafted to deal with unwanted emails.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Written up' sounds like drafting a report, but in a down clue it turns the word upside down.
explanation.definitionFit: Junk email sent in bulk to people who never asked for it is the classic unsolicited electronic message.

clue.text: Writer's run up, displaying liveliness

indicators.note: to run something up is to make it hastily, so the letters are knocked into another order

parts.note: a Biro is a ballpoint pen, something one writes with

explanation.surface: An author sprints uphill with plenty of energy.
explanation.walkthrough: Another reading is that 'run', R, moves up one place in this down entry. A Biro is the British everyday word for a ballpoint pen.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian-derived word means vigour and spirit, especially in a performance, so it signals vivacity.

clue.text: Behind a flightless bird, we're told

indicators.note: what we are told reaches us by ear, so only the sound counts

parts.note: the rhea is a large South American flightless bird

explanation.surface: Someone reports being stuck behind a bird that cannot fly.
explanation.walkthrough: In non-rhotic British speech the bird's name and the word for the back sound the same.
explanation.definitionFit: As a noun for one's backside, or as a word for the back part of anything, it matches posterior.

clue.text: Temperature dropped for Mike, guard at entrance and poachers' foe

indicators.note: one thing dropped in favour of another is swapped out, so one letter replaces another

parts.note: a gatekeeper guards the way in
T is the abbreviation for temperature
Mike is M in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A doorman named Mike, who chases off poachers, felt the temperature fall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Temperature dropped' reads as weather; it means the T is dropped and M takes its place.
explanation.definitionFit: On a country estate the person employed to protect game birds and deer is the natural enemy of those hunting illegally.

clue.text: Very good, very good, OK

parts.note: SO means very, as in 'so good', and stands for the whole phrase
repeated, the same short intensifier again

explanation.surface: Someone gushes about something, then the verdict is merely all right.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is the anticlimax: double praise collapses into a shrug.
explanation.definitionFit: Something merely adequate, neither good nor bad, is middling or passable, which is what lukewarm approval means.

clue.text: Elbows out cove to get rice wine and starters of marinated black olives

parts.note: a cove is an inlet, an arm of the sea
saki is a variant spelling of sake, Japanese rice wine

indicators.note: starters are what come first in a meal, so each word gives its opening letter

parts.note: opening letters

explanation.surface: Someone elbows their way out of a bay to fetch sake and some olive appetisers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cove' is also old British slang for a man, which suits the surface but not the parse; here it is the sea inlet.
explanation.definitionFit: Standing with hands on hips makes the elbows jut sideways, which is the posture the phrase describes.
